## DI-0301 continues: two threads, one system

Your Quality Analyst (QA) is back with the next piece of **DI-0301**, her data-integrity
self-assessment. Module 1 left her with an honest, mixed finding on **DED-0458** — the BECS
(Blood Establishment Computer Software) donor-eligibility determination she used as her first test
case. Two letters of ALCOA passed cleanly, one hid a trap, one passed with a nuance, and one —
"accurate" — is still an open question. She hasn't closed any of that. She's opened two new ones.

**Thread one.** She pulls BECS's own audit trail for DED-0458 — the underlying log of who touched
that record and when. It exists. It's switched on. And she asks the question this module exists to
teach: has anyone actually *reviewed* this audit trail, as part of reviewing the record itself — or
has everyone simply confirmed BECS "has an audit trail," nodded, and moved on? She checks the
obvious next question too: how often is this audit trail supposed to be reviewed? She can't find an
answer. Not a wrong answer — no answer. Nobody ever decided.

**Thread two**, separate system, same assessment. BECS requires a Quality sign-off before certain
actions go through — the kind of approval step this curriculum has mentioned since `csv-and-becs`,
always described loosely as "Quality approves it." Your QA has never looked at that sign-off
through the lens of what makes an electronic signature *actually* count as a signature, legally.
She wants to test it like an inspector would: is every signature genuinely tied to one person, used
only by that person, and administered so that no single person could forge or misuse someone
else's? No citations yet — just the question, stated plainly, the way she'll ask it of the systems
administrator next.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure both threads are circling. An audit trail that exists but is never reviewed is
functionally the same, from a patient-safety standpoint, as having no audit trail at all — the
evidence of tampering or error sits right there, unread, until an inspector finds it first. An
electronic signature that isn't genuinely tied to one accountable person is functionally the same
as an unsigned record — it *claims* someone reviewed or approved it, and that claim can't be
trusted. Both failures share a shape: the system *looks* like it has the control. Nobody has
confirmed the control actually does anything.

You already run the ITSM (IT service management) disciplines this needs, under different names.
**IAM (identity and access management)** is knowing exactly who can do what in a system, tied to
one accountable identity, never a shared login. **PAM (privileged access management)** is the
tighter version you already apply to sensitive accounts: credentials that can't be shared, guessed,
or reused, with a reviewable trail of who approved what and when — a change ticket's own approval
log, which you already treat as evidence, not decoration. **MFA (multi-factor authentication)** is
the closest everyday parallel to this module's other half: a password alone usually isn't enough
for anything sensitive, so you require a second, independent factor. The regulation below asks for
exactly that logic, applied to a signature instead of a login.

Here's where the regulated world demands more. In ordinary IT governance, "the approval box got
checked" is usually treated as sufficient proof an approval happened. For a CGMP (current good
manufacturing practice) record, that's not enough. The signature itself has to be legally
equivalent to ink on paper — provably tied to one specific person, at one specific time, meaning one
specific thing (review, approval, authorship), in a way that survives being challenged in an
inspection or in court. And the audit trail behind the record isn't an IT artifact nobody in Quality
needs to look at — it's evidence a reviewer is expected to actually read, the way they'd notice a
cross-out on a paper record.

## The rule in plain English

Three things are tangled into DI-0301's two threads, and this module pulls them apart one at a
time.

**First: an audit trail is a specific thing, not a vague synonym for "logging."** FDA (Food and
Drug Administration) defines it precisely, in the same 2018 guidance module 1 used: a secure,
computer-generated, time-stamped record that lets you reconstruct who created, changed, or deleted
an electronic record, and when. A good audit trail doesn't just say "something changed." It captures
enough — a user name, a timestamp, what the operation actually did — that you could rebuild the
whole story of a record's history from it alone.

**Second: reviewing that audit trail isn't a separate job handed off to someone outside Quality —
it's part of the same person's job as reviewing the record itself.** FDA's own guidance (this is
**guidance tier** — FDA's current thinking, "should" language) says the person responsible for
reviewing a record under CGMP should review the audit trail behind it at the same time, the same
way they'd notice a correction on a paper form. And how often? If a regulation already specifies a
review frequency for the underlying data, use that same frequency for the audit trail. If it
doesn't, use risk assessment — how critical is the data, how strong are the other controls around
it, how much would an error or a cover-up actually affect product quality. "Nobody decided" is not a
valid answer to either question, and that's exactly DI-0301's first finding here.

**Third: an electronic signature doesn't automatically count as a real signature just because it
exists in a database.** Part 11 (21 CFR Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures) sets
five specific controls — **11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200, 11.300** — and all five are **regulation
tier**: binding CFR (Code of Federal Regulations) text, not guidance. Together they require that a
signature clearly show who signed, when, and what the signature means; that it's technically welded
to its record so it can't be moved to a different one; that it's unique to one person and never
recycled; that it takes at least two distinct components to execute, not one; and that the
credentials behind it are managed so that no single person acting alone could misuse someone else's.
Meet all five, and FDA's own guidance says the electronic signature can stand in for a handwritten
one on any CGMP record. Miss one, and it can't — no matter how official the system looks.

## The actual text

Start with FDA's own definition of an audit trail, quoted verbatim from
`sources/fda-guidance/data-integrity-cgmp-qa-2018.md` (Section III, Question 1c):

> For purposes of this guidance, audit trail means a secure, computer-generated, time-stamped
> electronic record that allows for reconstruction of the course of events relating to the
> creation, modification, or deletion of an electronic record.

The same answer gives a concrete illustration of what a good one actually captures:

> For example, the audit trail for a high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) run should
> include the user name, date/time of the run, the integration parameters used, and details of a
> reprocessing, if any. Documentation should include change justification for the reprocessing.

HPLC (high performance liquid chromatography) is a lab technique Lakeshore doesn't run, but the
pattern transfers directly: a good audit trail for DED-0458 would show which BECS login touched the
record, exactly when, and — if anything about the eligibility determination was ever reprocessed or
corrected — what changed and why, with a justification attached. Not just "a change happened."

Now the reviewer question, Question 7, quoted in full — and this is the line that does the real
work in this module:

> Audit trail review is similar to assessing cross-outs on paper when reviewing data. Personnel
> responsible for record review under CGMP should review the audit trails that capture changes to
> data associated with the record as they review the rest of the record.

Read that twice. It doesn't say "have IT review the audit trail separately." It says the *same*
person who reviews the record — the reviewer who'd already be checking DED-0458's content — should
be checking its audit trail too, at the same time, the way they'd notice a correction scratched out
on a paper form. Audit-trail review isn't a parallel IT task. It's folded into the record review
that was already supposed to be happening.

And the frequency question, Question 8, quoted in full:

> If the review frequency for the data is specified in CGMP regulations, adhere to that frequency
> for the audit trail review... In these cases, you would apply the same review frequency for the
> audit trail.
>
> If the review frequency for the data is not specified in CGMP regulations, you should determine
> the review frequency for the audit trail using knowledge of your processes and risk assessment
> tools. The risk assessment should include evaluation of data criticality, control mechanisms, and
> impact on product quality.

Apply that directly to DI-0301's finding: Lakeshore never explicitly decided how often BECS's audit
trail gets reviewed. That's not automatically a violation — it's a gap in the decision itself. Maybe
a CGMP regulation already sets a review frequency for donor-eligibility records that should simply
carry over. Maybe none does, and a documented risk assessment needs to set one. Either path is fine.
What isn't fine is what actually happened: nobody asked the question, so the review frequency
defaulted to "whenever someone happens to look" — which is not a frequency at all.

### Reconciling 11.10(e) with this module's own depth

Here's a nuance worth getting exactly right, because `csv-and-becs` already planted half of it.
FDA's 2003 Part 11 guidance (*Scope and Application*) puts audit trails — 21 CFR 11.10(e) — on its
own enforcement-discretion list: FDA doesn't intend to specifically enforce Part 11's own
audit-trail clause. `csv-and-becs` named that and stopped there. It doesn't follow that nobody has
to review BECS's audit trail. The predicate rule — the CGMP regulation that already requires
Lakeshore's own records to be reviewed, the same kind of rule `csv-and-becs` modules 5 and 6 already
showed carrying the real weight behind BECS's validation requirement instead of 11.10(a) itself — is
what actually reaches the audit trail here too. FDA's 2018 guidance's Questions 7 and 8, above, are
that predicate-rule obligation made concrete: the record-review requirement that already applies to
DED-0458 is what requires someone to review its audit trail, whether or not Part 11's own clause
gets specifically enforced. Both facts are true at once — enforcement discretion on 11.10(e)
itself, and a real, binding review duty carried by the predicate rule underneath it. Full
predicate-rule doctrine — what decides which regulation reaches a given record at all — is
`predicate-rules-and-hybrid-systems`'s subject, next module. Here, just notice the pattern
repeating.

### The e-signature components, one at a time

Now the second thread. Quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/11.50.md`:

> (a) Signed electronic records shall contain information associated with the signing that clearly
> indicates all of the following:
>
> (1) The printed name of the signer;
>
> (2) The date and time when the signature was executed; and
>
> (3) The meaning (such as review, approval, responsibility, or authorship) associated with the
> signature.
>
> (b) The items identified in paragraphs (a)(1), (a)(2), and (a)(3) of this section shall be
> subject to the same controls as for electronic records and shall be included as part of any human
> readable form of the electronic record (such as electronic display or printout).

In practice: if a Quality reviewer pulls up DED-0458's approval on screen, or prints it, those three
facts — who, when, what the signature means — have to actually be visible there, not sitting in a
database column only a systems administrator could query. If an inspector can't see the signer's
name, the timestamp, and whether the signature means "I reviewed this" or "I approved this" just by
looking at the record, 11.50 isn't satisfied, no matter what the underlying data contains.

Next, `sources/cfr/11.70.md`, quoted in full:

> Electronic signatures and handwritten signatures executed to electronic records shall be linked to
> their respective electronic records to ensure that the signatures cannot be excised, copied, or
> otherwise transferred to falsify an electronic record by ordinary means.

This rules out a tempting shortcut: a signature that's really just a separate log entry saying
"User X approved record #458" — technically true, but with nothing stopping that same logged entry
from being pointed at record #459 instead, later, by anyone with access to the log. 11.70 requires
the link itself to be tamper-resistant, not just the signature's existence. A signature sitting in
its own table, referencing a record only by ID number with no technical barrier to re-pointing it,
fails this test even if every individual signature was genuine when made.

Now `sources/cfr/11.100.md`, the general requirements, quoted in full:

> (a) Each electronic signature shall be unique to one individual and shall not be reused by, or
> reassigned to, anyone else.
>
> (b) Before an organization establishes, assigns, certifies, or otherwise sanctions an individual's
> electronic signature, or any element of such electronic signature, the organization shall verify
> the identity of the individual.
>
> (c) Persons using electronic signatures shall, prior to or at the time of such use, certify to the
> agency that the electronic signatures in their system, used on or after August 20, 1997, are
> intended to be the legally binding equivalent of traditional handwritten signatures.

Three separate obligations: a signature can never be handed down to a replacement employee the way
a role-based login sometimes is; identity has to be verified *before* a signature is ever assigned,
not assumed; and the organization itself has to go on record with FDA, in writing, with an actual
handwritten signature, that its electronic signatures are meant to carry the same legal weight as
ink. That third piece is an organizational commitment, made once, not a per-record check — but it's
what makes every signature under it mean something legally in the first place.

Now `sources/cfr/11.200.md`, components and controls, quoted in full:

> (a) Electronic signatures that are not based upon biometrics shall:
>
> (1) Employ at least two distinct identification components such as an identification code and
> password.
>
> (i) When an individual executes a series of signings during a single, continuous period of
> controlled system access, the first signing shall be executed using all electronic signature
> components; subsequent signings shall be executed using at least one electronic signature
> component that is only executable by, and designed to be used only by, the individual.
>
> (ii) When an individual executes one or more signings not performed during a single, continuous
> period of controlled system access, each signing shall be executed using all of the electronic
> signature components.
>
> (2) Be used only by their genuine owners; and
>
> (3) Be administered and executed to ensure that attempted use of an individual's electronic
> signature by anyone other than its genuine owner requires collaboration of two or more
> individuals.

This is the MFA (multi-factor authentication) logic made regulatory: two distinct components for a
non-biometric signature — typically an ID code plus a password — with the first signing in a
session requiring both, and later signings in that same unbroken session allowed to use just the
one component that's uniquely tied to that person. And (a)(3) is the sharpest line in this whole
module: misuse of someone's signature has to require *two or more people acting together*. If one
person, acting entirely alone, could forge or misuse a colleague's signature, 11.200 isn't met —
full stop, regardless of how many components exist on paper.

Last, `sources/cfr/11.300.md`, controls for ID codes and passwords, quoted in full:

> Persons who use electronic signatures based upon use of identification codes in combination with
> passwords shall employ controls to ensure their security and integrity. Such controls shall
> include:
>
> (a) Maintaining the uniqueness of each combined identification code and password, such that no two
> individuals have the same combination of identification code and password.
>
> (b) Ensuring that identification code and password issuances are periodically checked, recalled,
> or revised (e.g., to cover such events as password aging).
>
> (c) Following loss management procedures to electronically deauthorize lost, stolen, missing, or
> otherwise potentially compromised tokens, cards, and other devices that bear or generate
> identification code or password information, and to issue temporary or permanent replacements
> using suitable, rigorous controls.
>
> (d) Use of transaction safeguards to prevent unauthorized use of passwords and/or identification
> codes, and to detect and report in an immediate and urgent manner any attempts at their
> unauthorized use to the system security unit, and, as appropriate, to organizational management.
>
> (e) Initial and periodic testing of devices, such as tokens or cards, that bear or generate
> identification code or password information to ensure that they function properly and have not
> been altered in an unauthorized manner.

Five separate controls, and five separate things an inspector could ask to see evidence of:
uniqueness, periodic revision (password aging named explicitly), a documented loss-management
procedure, active monitoring for unauthorized attempts, and periodic testing of any physical token.
A written policy that mentions password aging isn't the same as proof the aging actually happens —
and that gap is exactly where DI-0301's e-signature thread lands.

### Running the test against Lakeshore's BECS sign-off

Your QA walks the current setup through 11.100, 11.200, and 11.300 as a real test, not a formality.

**11.200's two-component requirement — holds up.** Every BECS approval genuinely requires an ID
code plus a password to execute the first signing in a session, exactly as (a)(1) requires. This is
a clean pass, and it's worth naming as one: not every finding in a self-assessment has to be a gap.

**11.100's uniqueness requirement — holds up, so far as she can verify.** Each signature traces to
one individual login, never shared, never reassigned when someone leaves — the identity-management
discipline this curriculum has already pressed on elsewhere, here applied to signatures
specifically.

**11.300(b)'s periodic revision — this is the gap.** Lakeshore's written password policy says
passwords must be changed on a set schedule. When your QA asks the systems administrator for
evidence this actually happens — a log of forced password changes, a configuration enforcing the
interval — he can't produce one. The policy was written. It was never technically enforced. Nobody
circled back to confirm the system was doing what the document said it would. That's a real,
documented-but-not-implemented gap: the kind an inspector finds fastest, by asking for evidence, not
a policy.

One holds up cleanly. One doesn't, despite being written down correctly. That's an honest finding,
not an overclaimed violation and not a false "it's fine."

Last, the question FDA's own 2018 guidance answers directly — Question 11, quoted verbatim:

> Yes, electronic signatures with the appropriate controls can be used instead of handwritten
> signatures or initials in any CGMP required record.

And its cited mechanism, from the same answer:

> ...an electronic signature with the appropriate controls to securely link the signature with the
> associated record fulfills this requirement (21 CFR 11.2(a)).

"Appropriate controls" isn't a vague phrase. It means satisfying 11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200, and
11.300 — not clicking an "I agree" button or typing a name into a text field. DED-0458's BECS
sign-off can only stand in for a handwritten signature to the extent it actually clears all five.
Right now, by DI-0301's own test, it clears four and has one documented gap.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) assessor
wouldn't ask whether Lakeshore has an audit-trail policy or an e-signature policy. They'd ask for
specific evidence, record in hand.

**For audit-trail review:** evidence the person reviewing DED-0458 also looked at its audit trail —
a review checklist that names it, a signed-off note referencing a specific change — not a general
statement that "BECS has an audit trail." A bad answer sounds like "the system logs everything
automatically." A good answer names a specific reviewer and a specific date the audit trail was
actually read.

**For review frequency:** a documented decision — either "this follows the same frequency as
§211.188(b)'s review" or "this was risk-assessed, and here's the assessment" — not silence. "We've
just always looked at it when something seemed off" is the answer DI-0301 is flagging, and it's the
one an inspector would flag too.

**For the e-signature setup:** a demonstration, not a description. Can the system show a signed
record with the signer's name, timestamp, and meaning on screen (11.50)? Can someone explain why a
signature can't be re-pointed at a different record (11.70)? Can the systems administrator produce
actual evidence — not a policy document — that passwords are periodically revised (11.300(b))? A bad
answer sounds like "our policy requires password changes every 90 days." A good answer produces the
log showing it happened.

## Common traps

**"Part 11's audit-trail requirement is on FDA's enforcement-discretion list, so nobody actually
has to review BECS's audit trail."** This is the trap this module exists to refute. FDA's 2003 Part
11 guidance does put 11.10(e) on its enforcement-discretion list — FDA doesn't intend to bring an
enforcement action specifically over Part 11's own audit-trail clause. But the predicate rule — the
CGMP record-review requirement that already reaches DED-0458 — carries the actual obligation to
review the audit trail behind that record. FDA's 2018 guidance's Questions 7 and 8, above, are that
obligation made concrete. Enforcement discretion on one clause doesn't erase a review duty sitting
underneath it on a different, binding rule.

**"We have an e-signature system, so our signatures are legally equivalent to handwritten ones."**
Not automatically. FDA's 2018 guidance says yes, an electronic signature *can* replace a handwritten
one — but only "with the appropriate controls," and that phrase has five specific regulatory
addresses: 11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200, 11.300. Lakeshore's BECS sign-off meets four of them
cleanly and has a real, documented gap in the fifth. "We have e-signatures" and "our e-signatures
satisfy Part 11's controls" are different claims, and only the second is what an inspector actually
asks about.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask your QA who reviewed BECS's audit trail for DED-0458, and when.** "BECS logs everything" is
  not an answer. A name and a date are.
- **Ask whether Lakeshore ever explicitly decided an audit-trail review frequency for BECS — and if
  the honest answer is no, treat that as the finding, not a crisis.** It's fixable with either a
  matched CGMP frequency or a documented risk assessment, not an automatic violation.
- **When someone tells you "Quality signs off on that in BECS," ask what makes that signature count
  as a signature** — can you see the signer's name, timestamp, and meaning on screen? Is it
  technically impossible to point that signature at a different record later?
- **Treat a written password-aging policy with no enforcement evidence as exactly the gap it is** —
  not a minor lapse. 11.300(b) asks for revision that actually happens, and "it's in the policy"
  isn't proof it does.
- **When a vendor says "our system is Part 11 compliant for e-signatures," ask which of the five
  sections they mean** — 11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200, or 11.300. A vague claim covering all five at
  once is usually covering none of them in enough depth to survive a real question.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Since FDA's 2003 Part 11 guidance puts audit trails on its enforcement-discretion list, does that mean nobody actually has to review BECS's audit trail?

No. FDA's 2003 guidance does say it doesn't intend to specifically enforce Part 11's own
audit-trail clause, 11.10(e). But the predicate rule — the underlying CGMP record-review
requirement that already reaches a record like DED-0458 — is what actually carries the obligation
to review the audit trail supporting it. FDA's 2018 guidance makes that obligation concrete:
personnel responsible for reviewing a record under CGMP should review its audit trail as they
review the rest of the record, at a frequency either matched to the data's own CGMP review
frequency or set by risk assessment. This is exactly the pattern `csv-and-becs` already taught for
validation: FDA's enforcement discretion applies to Part 11's own clause specifically, not to the
underlying predicate-rule duty, which still fully applies.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: DI-0301 finds that Lakeshore's written policy requires periodic password revision for BECS sign-off accounts, but nobody can produce evidence it actually happens. Is a written policy enough to satisfy 11.300(b)?

No — and this is worth stating plainly, because it's **not a regulatory requirement met by
documentation alone**. 21 CFR 11.300(b) requires that identification code and password issuances
actually be "periodically checked, recalled, or revised," with password aging named as the example.
A policy document saying this should happen is not evidence that it does. DI-0301's finding here —
the policy exists, the enforcement doesn't — is a real, specific gap under 11.300(b), not a
technicality, and it's exactly the kind of "documented but not implemented" finding a self-assessment
is supposed to surface before an inspector does.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Could one person at Lakeshore, acting entirely alone, forge or misuse a colleague's BECS e-signature?

By 21 CFR 11.200(a)(3)'s own standard, they shouldn't be able to — that section requires electronic
signatures to be "administered and executed to ensure that attempted use of an individual's
electronic signature by anyone other than its genuine owner requires collaboration of two or more
individuals." DI-0301's test of Lakeshore's current setup found this control genuinely holds: BECS's
two-component requirement (11.200(a)(1)) and its per-individual access controls mean misuse would
require more than one person's cooperation. This is one of the places this module's scenario found
a clean pass, not a gap — worth noticing precisely because not every finding needs to be a problem.
:::

## Where this goes next

DI-0301's second module closes with two honest findings: an audit-trail review frequency that was
never actually decided, and an e-signature setup that passes its two-component and misuse-resistance
tests cleanly but has a real, documented-but-unenforced gap in password revision. Next,
`predicate-rules-and-hybrid-systems` finally gives full depth to the term this module used once and
pointed past — **predicate rule**, the underlying regulation a Part 11 control protects — and asks
a harder question still open from module 1: when Lakeshore keeps both a paper and an electronic
version of a record, which one is actually the record of record?
